# A generic struct's literal takes the type arguments its fields say, on every
# target: `pair{k=1, v=3}` is a pair[int, int], as a generic function's
# arguments bind its own. It was a bare `pair`, so assigning it to a
# `pair[int, string]` was refused and a method taking its V, `larger(other=5)`,
# bound nothing: "cannot pass int as V".

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout '1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=html app.sngl
stdout '1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout '1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=fyne --language=go app.sngl
stdout '1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=gtk4 --language=go app.sngl
stdout '1 tests, 0 failures'

sngl test --platform=android --language=kotlin app.sngl
stdout '1 tests, 0 failures'

-- app.sngl --
import test "sngl:test"
import ui "sngl:ui"

struct pair[K any, V any] {
    k K
    v V
}

func pair[K any, V ordered].larger(this pair[K, V], other V) V {
    return this.v < other ? other : this.v
}

component page ui.node {
    ui.text("page")
}

func testALiteralBindsItsArguments(t test.Test, c page) {
    var p = pair{k=1, v=3}
    t.assert(p.larger(other=5) == 5)
    var q pair[string, string] = pair{k="a", v="b"}
    t.assert(q.v == "b")
}

ui.window {
    page()
}
